newsitem.title: UK: Key grain nations to meet in London this week.
newsitem.headline: Key grain nations to meet in London this week.

text.p: Food trading nations meet in London this week to discuss strategies as sliding prices and prospects of comfortable supplies promise fierce competition among key exporters.

U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman will be among policymakers to attend a London session on Thursday and Friday of the International Grains Council (IGC), a "club" of 44 leading grain importing and exporting nations.

The European Commission's deputy director for agriculature, David Roberts, will also be there. So will officials of other big exporters - Ralph Goodale, minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board, and Trevor Flugge, chairman of the Australian Wheat Board.

World wheat prices are now well below record levels of a year ago when stocks fell to 20-year lows. But weaker prices - below $3.50 per bushel in Chicago after $7.50 early in 1996 - have so far failed to spark a major buying spree from generally well-covered importers.
Easier prices reflect a better outlook for the U.S. wheat crop and prospects in Europe that have improved after beneficial rains in May.
Importers have held back, waiting for world prices to ease further.

In its report in early June, the IGC predicted that North African nations hit by drought and poor crops at home should turn active buyers in the new 1997/98 season. But so far only Egypt and Pakistan have taken advantage of lower prices.
Algeria, whose 1997 wheat production may fall to 1.6 million tonnes from 2.4 million last year, however, came up this week with a tender for 150,000 tonnes of optional milling wheat for July-August.

The latest statistics from the IGC also suggest that despite favourable crop prospects world wheat production for 1997 will decline by three million tonnes to 578 million. Consumption is forecast at 582 million, up five million over 1996.

Lower output in major producing nations such as Canada, Argentina, Australia, the United States and the European Union will be partly offset by a sharp rise from nations in eastern and central Europe.
World wheat trade is set to expand by two million tonnes to 93 million, partly driven by strong demand from North Africa.

The IGC also expects production of coarse grains - mainly maize (corn) - to jump by 11 million tonnes to 903 million, largely on a sharp rise in U.S. maize output. Consumption will hit a record 896 million tonnes.
The export strategy of the European Union, which removed itself from world markets in April when prices soared, should be under the spotlight during the grain talks.

The EU restored controversial taxes on wheat and flour exports in April to help control domestic supplies and prices in the face of volatile prices. But lower world prices and prospects of a good crop in Europe led it to scrap taxes last week, replacing them with short-validity licences whose value cannot be set in advance.

Exporters see the move as a first step towards resuming full blown exports and restoring export subsidies despite U.S. opposition. But the European Union has so far resisted calls for opening grain export tenders for the new season, out of caution ahead of the new crop.
U.S. officials attending the talks are likely to discuss these latest developments as the U.S. has repeatedly said EU taxes are just as bad as subsidies as they distort trade.
U.S. and EU policy makers are also likely to differ over genetically-modified organisms (GMOs).

The European Union has authorised the sale of gene-modified crops but is under pressure from consumer and retailing groups to label food containing GMO crops. But the United States has said separating gene-crops from other crops was unneeded and very expensive.
